title: Making smooth joins in air-dry clay
subtitle: The score, slip, and blend method for strong invisible joins
excerpt: A smooth join in air-dry clay relies on three things: mechanical roughening of both surfaces, a clay slip that penetrates the scratch marks, and thorough blending of the joined edges with a rib. Done correctly the join disappears; done incorrectly it cracks on drying.
sourceNotes: Score-and-slip joining technique derived from first principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: Roughening both clay surfaces with a needle, applying diluted clay (slip), and pressing the surfaces together for a strong mechanical and chemical bond
Clay diluted with water to a thick cream consistency; used as the bonding agent in joins
The ideal joining stage: the clay holds its shape firmly but is still damp enough for slip to bond effectively

content.text: The
score-and-slip
method is used across all hand-building techniques to join clay pieces. The score roughens the surface so the
slip
has scratches to key into; the slip is the adhesive; the blending removes the join line. All three steps are necessary.
When to use this technique

Score and slip is used any time two pieces of clay are joined: adding walls to a base, attaching a handle, joining two pinch pots rim-to-rim, attaching decorative sprigs or coils. Both pieces should be at matching moisture levels , ideally both
leather-hard
. Very soft to very dry joins fail , too-soft clay deforms; too-dry clay does not accept slip.
What you need
Needle tool (for scoring)
Clay slip: air-dry clay mixed with a little water to the consistency of thick yogurt
Wooden rib (for blending joins)
Damp sponge
Step-by-step

Score both surfaces. Use the needle tool to hatch a grid of shallow lines across the entire join area. Lines should cross at 45 degrees, about 2 mm apart, and penetrate 1-2 mm into the clay. More scratches give more surface area for the slip to key into.
Apply slip to both scored surfaces. The layer of slip should be visible but not thick enough to pool. Thin slip penetrates the score marks; thick slip sits on top and does not bond as well.

Press the two surfaces firmly together. Hold for 15-20 seconds so the surfaces have time to bond. You should feel a slight resistance when you try to pull them apart , this means the slip is doing its job.

Blend the join immediately on the inside face using a wooden rib pressed into the joint and drawn along it. Work in one direction, not back and forth, to push clay into the join rather than pulling it back out.
Blend the outside of the join. Smooth any excess slip with a damp sponge.
What a good join looks like

A properly blended join is invisible at leather-hard stage , no seam, no crack, no raised ridge. At bone-dry stage the join should be as strong as the surrounding clay; the piece should not flex or show a hairline at the join point. A good join holds the same density as the parent clay.
Common mistakes
Skipping scoring. Pressing two damp surfaces together with slip but without scoring creates a weak surface join. The roughened surface gives the slip mechanical grip.
Using water instead of slip. Water wets the surface but provides no bonding material. Slip carries clay particles that fill the gap between pieces.
Not blending the join. Pressing and leaving is not enough. The join line must be physically worked into the surrounding clay with a rib.
Joining pieces at mismatched dryness. A soft piece joined to a stiff one will crack as the soft piece shrinks more. Work pieces to matching moisture before joining.
